answer.label: Not John F. Kennedy — actually Robert F. Kennedy
answer.authorDates: 1925–1968 · U.S. Senator from New York & former Attorney General
answer.sourceLine: These are the words of Robert F. Kennedy, not his brother John. He delivered them in his report to the U.S. Senate on his 1966 trip to Latin America and the Alliance for Progress (Speech in the United States Senate, 9 May 1966 ↗), and later folded the passage into his 1967 book To Seek a Newer World. The line is persistently mis-credited to President Kennedy, whose own famous variation — “Those who make peaceful revolution impossible will make violent revolution inevitable” — is a different sentence from a different speech.

source.excerpt: A revolution is coming — a revolution which will be peaceful if we are wise enough; compassionate if we care enough; successful if we are fortunate enough — but a revolution which is coming whether we will it or not. We can affect its character; we cannot alter its inevitability.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced Robert F. Kennedy section ↗ places the exact wording in his “Speech in the United States Senate (9 May 1966).”
The American Presidency Project text ↗ of JFK’s 1962 address contains a different sentence, confirming this is not the president’s line.
WIST ↗ and Goodreads ↗ both attach the quote to RFK’s May 1966 Senate report, including the closing “affect its character…” sentence.
source.excerptNote: The closing pair of sentences — often dropped when the line is shared — is preserved in the sourced records.

author.heading: About Robert F. Kennedy
author.metaLine: 1925–1968 · U.S. Attorney General, Senator for New York & presidential candidate
author.bio: Robert Francis Kennedy served as U.S. Attorney General under his brother John and, after JFK’s assassination, as a senator from New York. His 1966 fact-finding trip to Latin America produced a widely quoted Senate report on the Alliance for Progress. He was assassinated in June 1968 while campaigning for the Democratic presidential nomination.

misattribution.heading: Right family, wrong Kennedy
misattribution.intro: Because both brothers spoke about the Alliance for Progress and “peaceful revolution,” this Robert F. Kennedy line is constantly reassigned to President John F. Kennedy on quote sites, memes and social posts.

items.why: The 35th president is the name most often stamped on this line, but the exact wording traces to Robert F. Kennedy’s 1966 Senate report, per Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ and WIST ↗. JFK’s genuinely comparable sentence is the separate “Those who make peaceful revolution impossible… ↗” from his 13 March 1962 address.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Robert F. Kennedy’s, from his 9 May 1966 Senate report on Latin America — later reused in his 1967 book To Seek a Newer World ↗.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Robert Kennedy delivered these words after touring Latin America, arguing that sweeping social change was inevitable and that the United States could shape whether it came peacefully or violently. The passage became one of the signature lines of his post-1963 political voice.

The confusion with his brother is easy to understand: John F. Kennedy launched the Alliance for Progress and used strikingly similar language about “peaceful revolution.” But the specific cadence — ‘wise enough… care enough… fortunate enough’ — belongs to Robert.
context.pull: We can affect its character; we cannot alter its inevitability.
